replies.author: @ChessMasterNate
replies.text:
If we don't produce something or much less than is required, almost certainly it can be shipped for less money.  That is a good thing.  When the world gets what we can make cheaper than anyone else and we get what they make cheaper than anywhere else, we all get more.
It is the same reason people began to specialize and have occupations in cities several thousand years ago, and why those cities prospered.
Peace and good relations are a boon for us all.  
Self-sufficiency might be a value, but it is a poor choice, if we can trade what we do best.
There are complications with this simplistic model.  It matters if the cheap producers in other countries are doing long-term damage to the planet.  Not reflecting the real cost.  And it matters if countries or colluding organizations like OPEC play politics and are given the power to make countries suffer from shock embargo.  And it can even matter, if the workers are suffering greatly, while a few owners make all the money, because those workers can revolt, and not only can supply stop but their anger can get directed at the countries receiving the product or substance, potentially leading to terrorism.
And, on top of all that we have to consider the effects of trade deficits.
So, trade is the more complex route, but it has better payoff.  And many of the risks presented can be mitigated by valuing and nurturing good relations, wise choices, critical reserves, and other planning ahead.
For example , when a mine goes under because it can't compete with foreign imports, we can prevent the sale to those who just want to scrap all the equipment and such.  The government can buy it and mothball the whole operation. Build concrete buildings to house all the equipment and protect it from corrosion and such.  Pump out any water that may damage the operation as if it were running. They can treat ground surfaces so environmental damage is minimal and it can easily and quickly be returned to full operation.  You, of course, would also have security people and inspectors that have good documentation of everything, and not the same inspectors for the same sites.  Constantly rotating and randomly.  So, valuable equipment does not turn up missing.  Monitoring from satellite can also be employed.
It would require some law changes, so creditors can't swoop in and take the equipment.
It currently costs too much money for the government to restore a mine to operational condition.  Keeping it in this preserved state, means you can get it operational at little more than normal operating costs, and the small cost of the protection over time.
